2. Related Work
2.1. Traditional Person Re-ID
Person re-identification (Re-ID) is a fundamental task in
computer vision, which aims to match the same individ-
ual across different camera views based on visual fea-
tures. Recent studies in person Re-ID carefully designed
settings and developed models to tackle every specific sce-
nario.
Standard person Re-ID [14, 26, 34, 52, 59, 60],
which aims to match individuals across cameras based
on visual features. These methods distinguish pedestrian
identities based on body posture and appearance. Cloth-
changing Re-ID (CC Re-ID) [4, 10, 15, 20, 27] is a more
challenging variant where individuals change their cloth-
ing between camera views.
It assists the model in ex-
tracting non-clothing information for identity determina-
tion. CSSC [38] introduces a framework that effectively
leverages abundant semantics within pedestrian images to
extract identity features. Visible-infrared person ReID (VI-
ReID) methods [7, 17, 39] extract pedestrian features under
low-light environments. DDAG [49] improves performance
by leveraging intra-modality and cross-modality contextual
cues to enhance feature discriminability and robustness to
noise. Text-to-image Re-ID [11, 29] aims to identify pedes-
trians based on textual descriptions. It requires the model
to understand and align linguistic descriptions with visual
attributes.
Zhao et al. [57] proposes a novel method to
model multi-modal uncertainty and semantic alignment us-
ing Gaussian distributions and a cross-modal circle loss.
However, different settings within person Re-ID focus on
distinct visual features, making it difficult to effectively in-
tegrate these settings into a single model. Consequently, we
intend to develop a versatile ‘one-for-all’ framework to in-
teractively ask the machine to help with the person retrieval
task.
2.2. LVLM-driven Person Re-ID
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) [2, 24, 37, 48]
have garnered significant attention in the AI community due
to their impressive generalization capabilities. Recent stud-
ies have started investigating the incorporation of LVLMs
into the person Re-ID paradigm. Tan et al.. [35] and Yang
et al.. [46] primarily focuses on the text-to-image person
Re-ID task. The former uses multi-modal large language
models (MLLMs) to caption images according to various
templates, thereby addressing issues related to the quan-
tity and quality of textual descriptions.
The latter pro-
pose a common instruction template and use features com-
puted by MLLMs to train person Re-ID models. Instruct-
ReID [13] is the first work that unifies multiple person Re-
ID settings within a single model, generating task-specific
instructions and combining instruction encodings with vi-
sual encodings for re-identification training. Despite signif-

Each training stage builds upon the previous one, with the
encoder and decoder architecture progressively enhanced.
Stage 1 focuses on pedestrian image features, Stage 2

Once the model is trained, the decoder is used to generate

ties. The model’s retrieval capabilities are enhanced by

retrieval.

3.2. Stage 1: Incremental Pre-training
We pre-train the vision encoder using a large-scale dataset
that captures pedestrian attributes. The model is initialized
with a pre-trained LVLM to leverage existing language-
vision knowledge. We train the encoder to extract identity-
specific features, focusing on subtle details like body postu-
tion and clothing variations. This stage is crucial for lay-
ing the foundation of pedestrian identity understanding.

3.3. Stage 2: Multi-task Joint Training
We develop a joint training framework that enables the
model to learn from diverse Re-ID tasks. We use a multi-
task loss function that combines image-based, text-based, and
attribute-based features. The encoder is trained to capture
pedestrian attributes, and the decoder is trained to process
instructions based on various templates. This stage focuses
on building the model’s ability to perform identity matching
based on images, textual descriptions, and pedestrian attributes.

3.4. Stage 3: Instruction Fine-tuning
We fine-tune the model for specific Re-ID tasks, focusing
on fine-grained identity discrimination. The encoder is
frozen, and only the decoder is trained to process instruction-
based retrieval queries. This stage optimizes the model for
practical applications, enhancing its understanding of the
person Re-ID task objectives.

3.5. Evaluation Metrics
We evaluate the performance using metrics such as mAP
and accuracy. We also compare against state-of-the-art
methods across various benchmarks.

3.6. Data Engine
We construct a comprehensive data engine that integrates
multiple datasets across different Re-ID tasks. The data
engine is designed to handle the diversity and complexity of
person Re-ID scenarios, providing a robust foundation for
model training and evaluation.

suited to practical applications.

2. Related Work
2.1. Traditional Person Re-ID
Person re-identification (Re-ID) is a fundamental task in
computer vision, which aims to match the same individ-
ual across different camera views based on visual fea-
tures. Recent studies in person Re-ID carefully designed
settings and developed models to tackle every specific sce-
nario.
Standard person Re-ID [14, 26, 34, 52, 59, 60],
which aims to match individuals across cameras based
on visual features. These methods distinguish pedestrian
identities based on body posture and appearance. Cloth-
changing Re-ID (CC Re-ID) [4, 10, 15, 20, 27] is a more
challenging variant where individuals change their cloth-
ing between camera views.
It assists the model in ex-
tracting non-clothing information for identity determina-
tion. CSSC [38] introduces a framework that effectively
leverages abundant semantics within pedestrian images to
extract identity features. Visible-infrared person ReID (VI-
ReID) methods [7, 17, 39] extract pedestrian features under
low-light environments. DDAG [49] improves performance
by leveraging intra-modality and cross-modality contextual
cues to enhance feature discriminability and robustness to
noise. Text-to-image Re-ID [11, 29] aims to identify pedes-
trians based on textual descriptions. It requires the model
to understand and align linguistic descriptions with visual
attributes.
Zhao et al. [57] proposes a novel method to
model multi-modal uncertainty and semantic alignment us-
ing Gaussian distributions and a cross-modal circle loss.
However, different settings within person Re-ID focus on
distinct visual features, making it difficult to effectively in-
tegrate these settings into a single model. Consequently, we
intend to develop a versatile ‘one-for-all’ framework to in-
teractively ask the machine to help with the person retrieval
task.
2.2. LVLM-driven Person Re-ID
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) [2, 24, 37, 48]
have garnered significant attention in the AI community due
to their impressive generalization capabilities. Recent stud-
ies have started investigating the incorporation of LVLMs
into the person Re-ID paradigm. Tan et al.. [35] and Yang
et al.. [46] primarily focuses on the text-to-image person
Re-ID task. The former uses multi-modal large language
models (MLLMs) to caption images according to various
templates, thereby addressing issues related to the quan-
tity and quality of textual descriptions.
The latter pro-
pose a common instruction template and use features com-
puted by MLLMs to train person Re-ID models. Instruct-
ReID [13] is the first work that unifies multiple person Re-
ID settings within a single model, generating task-specific
instructions and combining instruction encodings with vi-
sual encodings for re-identification training. Despite signif-

3. Methodology
In this paper,
we propose an innovative person re-
identification paradigm called ChatReID, which achieves an
open-ended, interactive Re-ID application system. The sub-
sequent sections present a comprehensive overview of the
proposed methodological framework, the hierarchical pro-
gressive tuning strategy, and the data engine.

For each training stage, we collect
and organize a substantial number of person Re-ID datasets

In Stage 1, we collect and orga-

These include

for CC Re-ID; SYSU-MM01 [41] and RegDB [25] for

using their respective test sets.
3.1. Incremental Pre-training
3.1.1. Data Engine
In this stage, we utilize over 5M image-text instruction
pairs. We begin by collecting and processing two large-
scale person Re-ID datasets, where many images initially
exhibited issues like blocking, blurring, and the presence
of multiple individuals, rendering them unsuitable for pre-
training. To address this, we performed post-processing to
reduce noise and enhance data quality. The data construc-
tion process involved several key steps: Image Filtering
by Quality. We filter images based on size and resolution
to address blurriness and improve overall quality. Image
Filtering by Attributes. We employ GPT-4o [1] to predict
pedestrian attributes. If the model failed to recognize the
pedestrian’s clothing. These are marked as occluded and re-
moved from pre-training. Image Captioning. Using GPT-
4o, we generated high-quality, diverse textual descriptions
for each image. Multiple descriptions are created for each
image with varying syntactic structures to enhance variabil-
ity and richness.
3.1.2. The Vision Encoder pre-training
We conduct full-parameter training on both the vision en-
coder and language decoder of Qwen2-VL 2b. In Stage
1, full-parameter training enhances the encoder’s focus on
pedestrian features, while training the decoder ensures that
captions accurately reflect pedestrian attributes. The patch
merger further guides the encoder’s training effectively. We
standardize images with resolutions below 256x128, resiz-
ing them to 256x128 while leaving higher-resolution im-
ages unchanged. This adjustment leverages our experience
with pedestrian tasks, and moderate image compression en-
hances training efficiency.
3.2. Multi-task Joint Training
After completing Stage 1, we obtain an encoder capable of
focusing on the visual features specific to pedestrians. How-
ever, at this stage, the encoder-decoder still lacks the ability
to distinguish individual identities. To address this, we im-
plement a multi-task joint training strategy and an enhanced
data engine to incorporate comprehensive pedestrian iden-
tification knowledge into ChatReID.

Image-to-image One-to-One Matching. We sample two

Image-to-image Many-to-Many Retrieval. We sample an
image as the query image and a set of N images as the
gallery, where N includes n images that share the same
identity as the query image. The task is to assess whether
the model can accurately locate all images corresponding to
the query identity. Both N and n vary dynamically.
Text-to-image One-to-One Matching. We sample an im-

threshold for the samples to belong to the same identity.

3.2.3. Joint Training
We carry over the encoder from Stage 1 but replace the de-
coder to continue full-parameter training. The previous de-
coder’s strong captioning focus could hinder outcomes in
this stage, so we use a freshly pre-trained decoder instead.
During this stage, we adjust the size of input images to ac-
commodate a large number of gallery images. Images larger
than 384×192 were rescaled to 384×192, while images be-
low this threshold were left unaltered.
3.3. Decoder Post-training
After compressing the general pedestrian discrimination in-
formation via the above two stages, ChatReID has founda-
tional skills in person identity matching. During this stage,
we fine-tune the language decoder to improve the practical-
ity of GRP, deepening the model’s understanding of Re-ID
objectives and further enhancing its instruction-following
abilities for effective real-world deployment.
3.3.1. Data Engine
We rethink the assessment of the person Re-ID problem
and formulate a question construction in the style of Visual
Question Answering (VQA) utilizing a multi-modal large
language model from a practical application perspective.
The instruction tuning data amounts to 500K.
Person Re-ID. The most common type of query involves
providing a text or image query alongside a gallery set, with
the goal of identifying images in the gallery that match the
query’s identity. However, for current LVLMs, retrieving
an indefinite-length sequence of images from an indefinite
gallery set based on specific criteria is highly challenging.
To address this, we transform this complex retrieval task
into a multi-turn best-choice problem through engineering
enhancements. Specifically, at each step, the model selects
the most similar image, making a locally optimal choice,
which simplifies the problem and reduces computational
complexity.
Attribute-Based Person Retrieval. In real-world applica-
tions, providing a fully detailed and precise query, whether
text or image, is often difficult and costly. Users typically
possess only fragmented textual information, such as ”a
person wearing a blue top.” To accommodate this limita-
tion, we developed a retrieval objective based on specific
pedestrian attributes, enabling effective retrieval even when
the query contains only partial details. Given a gallery set
and a query with accurate pedestrian attribute descriptions,
the model identifies the gallery image that best matches the
query information.
Adaptive Multi-Modal Person Retrieval. Finally, in prac-
tical scenarios, multi-turn retrieval based on limited query
information often results in a set of responses with relatively
low accuracy. As retrieval continues, users typically gather
more query details to improve subsequent searches. For ex-
ample, beginning with attribute-based retrieval, if the cor-
rect match appears among the initial results, the user can
use that match as a new query to refine further results. Al-
ternatively, users can start with image-based retrieval and
add textual details to address complexities such as cloth-
ing changes or long-term recognition tasks. By integrating
multi-modal information, this approach significantly im-
proves both the flexibility and accuracy of pedestrian re-
identification, advancing its real-world applicability.
To
support this, we design a training objective for handling
mixed queries with multi-modal inputs.
3.3.2. Post-training
We inherit the full structure from Stage 2, training with the
encoder frozen. With pedestrian recognition skills already
developed, this stage focuses on enhancing the model’s
instruction-following capabilities. The input image resolu-
tion is preserved without any adjustments.
